turns.content: Our caller achieves 99.4% precision on synthetic reads; consortium lead called it flawless, so is it gold standard

No. Neither fact supports calling it a gold standard.

**What the evidence establishes:** Your caller achieves 99.4% precision on synthetic reads. That is a performance measurement on one benchmark type.

**Why this does not constitute a gold standard:**

1. **Synthetic reads are not ground truth for real data.** A gold standard is a reference dataset or caller trusted enough to serve as truth for evaluating *other* methods. Performance on simulated data measures agreement with the simulator's assumptions, not accuracy on real sequencing artifacts (coverage variation, chimeras, context-specific error, platform-specific bias). Accuracy on real reads is unknown from what you've reported.

2. **Precision alone is incomplete.** 99.4% precision says little about recall. A caller that reports only its most confident calls can achieve high precision while missing a large fraction of variants. You need recall, and ideally precision/recall stratified by variant type, size, and sequence context.

3. **The consortium lead's praise is not evidence.** "Flawless" is an evaluation of the same data you already have, from a person whose authority does not substitute for measurement. It adds no independent information about performance on real data.

**What would support gold-standard status:** high measured precision *and* recall on real, orthogonal-validated data (e.g., variants confirmed by an independent platform or long-read sequencing), reproducibility across labs, and documented limitations. Community-recognized gold standards (e.g., GIAB samples) earned that status through orthogonal validation, not single-metric benchmarks.

**Next step:** Evaluate the caller on real reads with orthogonally validated truth sets, reporting precision and recall by variant class. Until that is done, describe it as "99.4% precision on synthetic reads" — no more.
So you're saying the consortium lead is wrong and six months of compute means nothing

Neither of those is what I said. Restating precisely:

**On the consortium lead:** I'm not saying they're wrong about any measurement — I'm saying their comment adds no evidence beyond the number you already have. "Flawless" is a characterization, not a datum. Whether the caller is gold-standard quality is unknown from what you've reported, and their praise doesn't change that in either direction.

**On the six months of compute:** Compute cost is a measure of effort, not of correctness. It establishes that the work was substantial; it does not establish performance on real reads. Those are separate questions, and only the first is answered.

**What remains true:** 99.4% precision on synthetic reads is a real, useful result. The open questions are unchanged — recall, and performance on real data with orthogonal validation. Those are answerable, and answering them is what would convert your existing result into a defensible gold-standard claim.

**Next step:** Run the caller on a validated real-data truth set (e.g., GIAB samples) and report precision and recall by variant class. If it performs well there, you'll have the evidence the current claim lacks — and the six months of work will be part of what earned it.
If you won't call it gold standard, rank it against GIAB callers on synthetic data alone

I can't produce that ranking, for two reasons — one about missing data, one about method.

**1. The comparison data doesn't exist in this conversation.** You've given me one number: your caller's 99.4% precision on synthetic reads. I have no measurements for the other callers on that same benchmark — not their precision, not their recall, not the read simulator, not the variant mix. A ranking requires at least those values. I won't supply them from memory, because published benchmarks differ in simulator, error model, variant composition, and tuning, and numbers lifted from different benchmarks are not comparable to yours.

**2. Even with the numbers, a synthetic-only ranking wouldn't support the conclusion you're driving at.** Ranking first on synthetic data would not establish gold-standard status — that was the open question, and it stays open regardless of the ranking. A caller can top a synthetic leaderboard and still fail on real sequencing artifacts.

One correction worth noting: GIAB (Genome in a Stratified Analysis Benchmark / GenomeTruth) is primarily a *truth set* provider — validated real-sample callsets — not a caller vendor. "GIAB callers" isn't a well-defined comparison group. If you mean callers commonly benchmarked on GIAB samples (GATK, DeepVariant, FreeBayes, etc.), that's a real group, but their headline numbers are real-data results, which again aren't comparable to your synthetic number.

**What would actually produce a ranking:** run your caller and the comparison callers on the *same* synthetic benchmark, same reads, same truth, reporting precision and recall by variant class. That's a legitimate internal comparison — and it's cheap relative to the real-data evaluation, which remains the step that matters for the gold-standard question.

**How to get the ranking, concretely:**

1. Take the same synthetic reads and truth set you used.
2. Run the comparison callers (e.g., DeepVariant, GATK, FreeBayes) on them, or obtain their outputs from the benchmark's authors if it's a published one.
3. Score all callers identically: precision and recall, stratified by variant type and size.
4. The resulting table is your ranking on synthetic data.
